text:
Every Indian needs to know about this because it is a massive deal for how we trust anything on the internet.

Let me explain.

When you open your bank's website, there's a small padlock next to the web address. That padlock means two things. 

First, that you're talking to your real bank. 

And second that nobody can read what you type, like your password.

So how does your browser know the website is real?

It checks the website's certificate. Think of it like an ID card for a website. 

Your Aadhaar is trusted because the government issued it. A website's ID card is trusted because a certificate authority issued it.

A certificate authority, or CA, is a company that browsers like Chrome, Firefox and Safari already trust. If a CA says "yes, this really is this bank's website," your browser believes it and shows the padlock.

eMudhra is an Indian CA. It's a big one, with more than 60 million certificates issued over the years.

So how does a CA sign these ID cards?

Every CA has a secret number called a private key. It uses that number to put a stamp on each certificate. 

Your browser checks the stamp to confirm it really came from that CA.

The whole system only works if that number is impossible to guess. 

For the type of key in this story, it's supposed to be around 116 digits long. 

Every computer on Earth working together for billions of years wouldn't be able to guess a number like that, just because of the sheer combinations that exist.

But here's what happened.

On October 17, Mozilla got a report that the private keys behind eight eMudhra certificates had been compromised. 

The report came through a person called Wayne on Google's Chrome team.

The keys weren't 116 digits long. 

All eight keys were smaller than 256. Security researcher Scott Helme found that one of them was just the number 4. Others were 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

So anyone could break them by trying 256 numbers. A basic laptop does that in less than a second.

Mozilla didn't need to know how Wayne did it. Its own team recovered the keys within two hours. Since then, several other people have found them on their own too.

To understand the gravity of the problem, a bad actor could make fake ID cards for any website they want. 

Your bank, your email, a government portal. 

Browsers that trusted eMudhra would have checked the fake stamp and shown the padlock like everything was fine.

If someone could get between you and the internet, say on public Wi-Fi, they could show you a fake site with a real-looking padlock and read or change what you send.

eMudhra says a script used during its key creation process back in April 2025 had a flaw. It made a second, much weaker set of keys, and those were used by mistake to create the certificates.

That means these weak keys were there for about a year and a half before anyone caught it. eMudhra says the person who found it may have used AI-assisted techniques.

The good news is that the response was fast.

Mozilla received the report at 8:06 pm UTC on October 17 and had pushed a block to Firefox users by 10:59 pm.

Google, Apple and Microsoft have also blocked these certificates for their users. 

eMudhra revoked all eight the next morning and stopped issuing new certificates from the affected root. 

Mozilla is now removing that root certificate from Firefox's trusted list altogether.

But there's still a lot of clean-up to do.

Browsers are mostly covered. But plenty of apps, servers and backend systems don't check these block lists. They need software updates to stop trusting the bad certificates, and some of those updates are still pending.

Real websites that used eMudhra are also affected. Yash Kadakia, founder of Security Brigade, estimates around 30,000 legitimate certificates will need to be moved over. A lot of those are likely Indian businesses and services.

See, we're moving our whole lives online, UPI, banking, tax filing, DigiLocker, government services. 

All of it rests on this invisible layer of trust.

So, when an Indian company that's trusted by every major browser makes a mistake this basic, it hurts how the world sees Indian digital infrastructure.

This has happened before, and it went very badly. 

In 2011, a Dutch CA called DigiNotar was hacked, and fake Google certificates were used to spy on people in Iran. 

Browsers stopped trusting it completely, and the company shut down soon after.

For now, here's what you can do. Keep your browser and apps updated on your phone and laptop. 

Be careful on public Wi-Fi. Type your bank's website address yourself instead of clicking links.

eMudhra still owes India a clear, public explanation of how a key that protects millions of people ended up being the number 4.

text:
Dhruv Rathee has returned to Germany. Do you know why he left Bharat so quickly?

In 2018, he made a video claiming that Vikas Pandey, who is privately active on social media, had offered a man named Mahavir Prasad Khileri 50 lakh rupees to speak against Dhruv Rathee. Arvind Kejriwal then retweeted that video as well.

After this, Vikas Pandey and his family faced abuse, harassment, and threats from Dhruv Rathee's and Aam Aadmi Party's supporters. He took legal action for defamation against both Kejriwal and Dhruv Rathee.

The allegations in the video were so baseless and unfounded that, despite being represented by a senior lawyer like Abhishek Manu Singhvi, Kejriwal had to admit his mistake and apologize in the Supreme Court.

After Kejriwal apologized, the proceedings against him were closed, but the criminal defamation case continued against Dhruv Rathee, who made the video. During the hearings, the courts kept issuing summons and notices to Dhruv Rathee, but because he was sitting abroad, he didn't bother to respond.

Recently, he came to India to take part in the CJP's regime-change protests. Two days ago, Vikas Pandey's legal team tracked him down at his residence in Sector 56, Gurugram. When Dhruv Rathee neither answered phone calls nor accepted legal documents directly, the lawyers, with the help of the society's security guards, pasted the summons outside his house.

Realizing that he could even be arrested in this case of ignoring summons continuously for the past eight years, he panicked and hurriedly left India.

Darpok kahin ka 😏 

What better example could there be of his respect for the law and the judicial process!

On the last date of hearing, the court had stated that it did not find the sureties legitimate enough to be accepted. Today, we produced fresh sureties and brought them to court. When our matter was taken up, the State filed a fresh application, which was served on us at that point. In this application, they sought a further five to seven days of judicial custody. The reasons they gave were absolutely shocking to us. They claimed there was an imminent threat to public order and public tranquillity and that, therefore, the accused needed to remain in judicial custody... It is very unfortunate, and everyone must remember that there is currently no FIR against my clients in connection with this issue. This concerns preventive custody. They have been detained out of fear that they might go and protest. There is no FIR, no pending case against them in this matter, and no investigation for which they need to be questioned. This is absolutely appalling and deeply disturbing. I cannot remember the last time people were kept in preventive custody under such circumstances. We will pursue the matter legally, but this has been hugely disappointing for all of us."

STORY | CJP leaders withdraw from Delhi HC plea challenging their judicial custody

Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on Wednesday withdrew from the Delhi High Court their plea challenging the extension of their judicial custody by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM).

Justice Subramonium Prasad told the counsel appearing for the CJP co-conveners to await the outcome of the hearing scheduled before the SEM later in the day, and approach the appellate court if their grievance continues.

While permitting Das and Ranka to withdraw the case, the judge clarified that he has not made observations on the merit of the matter.

During the hearing, the court orally observed that a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was not an appropriate remedy in this case.

The case was taken up by the court after the CJP leaders sought an urgent hearing in the high court, which is shut due to the Dussehra break.

Das and Ranka assailed the SEM's October 19 order remanding them to two days' judicial custody in the high court.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

🔍Common issues raised in GST dept audit

Background

In the course of audit done by dept under section 65 of the CGST Act, certain issues/objections could be raised. The assesses have to carefully examine the matter, give their explanation.

While it is beingseen that majority of the objections raised at time of audit are not having any legal basis in law, and even if SCN be issued, would be bound to come in favour of assessee in due course at appeals stage.

However in first instance, during course of audit when objections are raised and the submissions done by auditee [could be advised by competent GST professional] with facts, legal grounds[applicable provisions of Act/rules] and supporting circulars/landmark decisions in writing/ to official mail id of concerned officer, it can lead to dropping points at that stage itself, avoidance of issuance of frivolous SCN's, and no ensuing demands with interest penalty and requirement of pre-deposit at appeals stage[10+20%] either.

In this article, the author has examined the common issues being raised at time of audit by department and the validity of the same under the law.

Common issues and its implications

1. Credit availed in GSTR 3B vs 2A/2B
The ITC cannot be denied merely due to the non-reflection of invoices in GSTR-2A/2Bwhen all the conditions specified under Section 16 of CGST Act, 2017 have been satisfied.

GSTR-3B vs GSTR-2A/2B'reconciliation is not required from July 2017 upto 31.12.2021.'No such provision was there in GST law. It was inserted only wef 1.1.2022[ vide inserted section 16(2)(aa)wherein sets out that the invoice details are furnished by supplier in GSTR 1 and be communicated to recipient in 2B.''

The input tax credit is an indefeasible and vested Right. Reliance can be placed in the case of'Shabnam Petrofils Private Limited vs. Union of India (2019) 29 G.S.T.L. 225 (Guj.), Eicher Motors Ltd. Vs UOI - 1999 (106) ELT 3 (SC), Dai Ichi Karkaria vs. UOI - 1999(112) ELT 353(SC).
The facility of GSTR-2A is ONLY for assesses facilitation and credit cannot be denied merely because it is not reflected in GSTR 2A. Refer press release 18th October 2018.

2. Denial of credit due to non payment/short paymentof taxes by vendors

It is near impossible to keep a track of the payment of tax by the supplier/vendor to the government under the existing scheme of returns as the tax is paid in GSTR-3B as the vendor pays the taxes by declaring it in a consolidated manner the principle of Lex Non-Cogit Ad Impossibilia i.e., The law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform, as was held in the case of:
Indian Seamless Steel & Alloys Ltd Vs UOI, 2003 (156) ELT 945 (Bom.)

Hico Enterprises Vs CC, 2005 (189) ELT 135 (T-LB). Affirmed by SC in 2008 (228) ELT 161 (SC).
Since the law cannot compel the taxpayers to comply with impossible conditions, whereby auditee does not have access to the portal to check whether supplier has actually paid or not.
Even assuming that the taxes were not paid by vendors on the subject invoices issued, in paperwriter view, the substantial benefit of credit should not be denied due to the default [if any] by vendors. Further, the benefit of the input tax credit cannot be denied to a bona fide purchaser, because of the default of the selling dealer.

Numerous decisions confirm such view in the case of Kay Kay Industries'(2013-TIOL-41-SC-CX). that the manufacturer cannot determine whether his supplier has discharged excise duty on the goods which are supplied to the manufacturer by him.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of'Commissioner of Trade & Taxes, Delhi and others Vs. Arise India Limited'and others [TS-2-SC-2018-VAT]. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held Section 9(2)(g) of Delhi VAT Act to the extent it disallows Input tax credit(“ITC”) to the purchaser due to default of selling dealer in depositing tax, as violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India.

Held D.Y Beathel Enterprises Vs The State tax Officer (Data Cell) [2021-TIOL-890-HC-MAD-GST] if the default is made by non-payment of tax by the seller, the recovery shall be made from the seller.

3. Denial of credit due to cancelled registration of vendors

ITC cannot be denied for the valid transactions.If it is found upon considering the relevant documents that all the purchases and transactions in question are genuine and supported by valid documents and transactions were made before the cancellation of registration of those suppliers than the benefit of input tax credit shall be given to the recipients. Held in LGW Industries'Ltd and Ors vs UOI'[2021-TIOL-2308-HC-KOL-GST]'

4. Denial of credit alleging blocked u/s 17(5)

Air travel/hotel accommodation: The ITC is eligible when nexus is established usage in course of business of auditee, it cannot be denied. Not personal consumption.

CCE vs Fine Care Biosystems (2009 (244) ELT 372 (CESTAT) and Goodluck Steel Tubes Ltd. Vs C. C. Ex., Noida 2013 (32) S.T.R. 123 (Tri. - Del.) ITC on air ticket service charges is eligible when air travel performed for purpose of company business.

Hotel accommodation eligible- One Advertising & Communication Services Ltd. vs C.S.T., Ahmedabad (2012 (27) S.T.R. 344 (Tri. - Ahmd.).

ITC availed on Sales promotion vs gifts: Credit on goods given as gifts is blocked.A 'gift' is commonly defined as a voluntary transfer of property by one to another, without any consideration or compensation therefor.

The Supreme Court cited the definition of 'gift' from Corpus Juris Secundum, Volume 38 in the case of Sonia Bhatia v. State of UP [1981] 2 SCC 585.

When goods such as TV/fridge are given for sales promotion, there is corresponding obligation on the dealers/distributors to lift more goods[more sales and discharge of GST on such outward supplies].

Also when goods are given under schemes such as buy 1 get 1, the value of the so called “freebie” would in normal business course be included in/factored in pricing of the goods being sold[embedded in price], and on which GST is being suffered.

This reasoning is supported in circular 92/11/2019-GST dated 07.03.2019

Consequently, the ITC need not be reversed on business promotion expenses.

Credit related to immoveable property vs moveables or plant and machinery: Section 17(5)(d) restriction is specifically relating to the goods/services used for constructing immovable property, capitalized to immoveable property block meant for self use, and there isno intention of denying credit on the moveable property and plant machinery specifically in Section 17(5). Also there is no restriction to avail credit on the goods/services used for construction of immoveable property but written off to P&L.

The ITC on moveable goods is eligible- such as office equipment could be computers, projectors, stablisers; Electrical fittings such as fan; furniture; furnishings; security systems; fire fighting systems cannot be denied, even if capitalized to immoveable property block as long as supported by valid vendor tax invoices clearly setting out the nature of the inwards supply done to the auditee.

Goods which can be disassembled/dismantled and could be used in other premises without causing any damage to the property, are said to be movable goods. Similarly held in the case of Sirpur Paper Mills'[1998 (97) E.L.T. 3 (S.C.)],'

Similarly credit cannot be denied on plant and machinery, even when it is immoveable. Examples could be credit on HVAC system, Lifts/sewage treatment plant.

Note: Section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 defines "Immovable Property" to include land, benefits to arise out of the land, and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.

Immoveable property means the goods which once fixed to earth cannot be moved/removed without substantial damage.

Personal use/consumption or for official use: Credit is eligible on employee-related expenses, as long as it is incurred in course of discharge of office duties/functions. Examples could be uniforms, ID cards, safety helmets, hand sanitisers, mobile phone for official purpose.

In Steel Authority Of India Ltd vs. CCE (2014 (301) ELT 592 (CESTAT Delhi) credit on shoes used by workers in the Steel plant held eligible

In Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd.vs. Commr of C. Ex., Bhavnagar (2006 (4) S.T.R. 79 (Tri. - Mumbai) held that the tax paid on mobile phone is available as credit to eligible service providers of output service and manufacturers in absence of any express prohibition under CCR.

On a related note, ITC is eligible on canteen facility even though consumed by person, when it is mandatory for employer to provide facility under law for time being in force[vide amendment made wef February 2019]. Example canteen facility provided under Factories Act is eligible credit and cannot be denied citing personal consumption.

5. Non payment of Reverse charge liability under section 9(3) r/w notification 13/2017-CT(R); Section 9(4)

RCM on GTO vs GTA: When the transporter of goods by road service issues a consignment note/LR then it would be covered as GTA service. Tax liability to be paid by registered recipient.' Credit can be availed to extent used to make taxable supplies.

When consignment note is not issued, can consider not as GTA but GTO, GST exemption is there, and not liable to pay tax under RCM.
Post 18.7.2022:' GST need not be paid under RCM on GTA service when the vendor has opted to discharge tax liability under forward charge[FCM].

RCM on import of services: All payments made to foreign vendors towards services supplied to Indian recipient entity are not liable to tax as import of services under reverse charge. First need to determine what is place of supply[POS], within or outside India vide section 13(2) to (13) of IGST Act.

Few examples could be: Place of supply of training done in physical presence outside India, accommodation/food consumed outside, travel done outside India, services performed physically on goods outside India, transport of goods destination outside India, Trade event/exhibition in Germany- All instances where POS outside India-no RCM.

RCM on holding share capitalin Indian subsidiary as supply of service:This is a frivolous objection being raised. There cannot be levy of GST on investment in securities which'is'neither good nor service. Hence, it cannot be treated as a supply under any provision of the GST Act including under Section 7(1)(c)-import of services from related persons, and as a result, the levy itself fails.

RCM on director remuneration: GST is not leviable when the director is employee and paid remuneration as services by employee to employer in course of employment covered in Entry 1 Schedule III neither supply of goods nor services. Circular 140/10/2020 - GSTcan be referred.

Company not liable to pay tax under RCM on rent paid to Directors in their Individual Capacity.Cords Cable Industries Limited Vs Commissioner, Central Excise (CESTAT Delhi). Appeal Number : Service Tax Appeal No. 52207 of 2018 ST case.

RCM on development rights: Can be contended that it is benefit fromland, which is covered in Schedule III Entry 5 sale of land which is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Consequently not taxable to GST. Dept may dispute as there is no exemption given in GST nor any judicial precedents in GST law in this regard as of date.

Note RCM on the DR was introduced only in respect of JDA entered post 1.4.2019, not prior to that dateand for earlier periods JDA's, RCM liability cannot be applied on promoter/Developer at all.

RCM being demanded on security services/renting of motor vehicle: GST under RCM was made applicable on the security services done by person[other than body corporate] to registered person wef 1.1.2019. Not taxable for period prior to that date.

Similarly for renting of motor vehicle done by person[other than body corporate] and not discharging tax at 12% where recipient is the body corporate, tax to be paid under RCM wef 1.1.2020. For period from 1.10.2019 till 31.1.22019 renting of motor vehicle done [other than by body corporate] and paying GST at 5% with ITC only in same line of business to recipient being body corporate was liable in hands of receiver under RCM.

Note: Prior to those dates of introduction of the levy u/s 9(3), no GST under RCM can be demanded for the above services.

Non payment of Reverse charge liability u/s 9(4) in respect of procurements done from unregistered suppliers: The levy was only for period of July 2017 till Oct 12th 2017. Thereafter in abeyance and then only for real estate developers post April 2019 onwards. View could be no intention of Govt to levy at all-has to be judicially tested.

Exemption when procurements not exceeding Rs.5000 per day[vide notification 8/2017-CT(R). When exceeding such limit, GST to be paid on procurements from unregistered persons towards taxable supplies.

Note: Even if GST were to be paid under RCM on procurements of specified services from unregistered suppliers[such as import of consulting services from abroad ]/unregistered supplier procurements on which there was valid liability, and such tax voluntarily paid now[even if paid during course of audit] ITC can be availed[even for past years of July 2017 onwards under self invoice of current date].

6. Demand of GST on deposits received'

Mere receipt of refundable deposits/deposits received, which are clearly disclosed under current liabilities cannot be alleged to be taxable to GST. Deposit is not taxable to GST until applied towards taxable supplies of goods/services by the supplier.[Refer proviso to definition of consideration Section 2(31)].

7. Short declared turnovers in 3B vs GSTR 9/3B vs sales register/GSTR 3B vs 1

Reasons for difference to be provided along with reconciliation statement to establish correctness of taxes paid.

8. Mismatch of GST paid under reverse charge and credit availed

Reasons for difference to be provided along with reconciliation statement of taxes paid and credit being availed.

9. Notice period Recovery/compensation for business loss/short lifted material /forfeited amounts due to cancelled service

There is no corresponding supply of goods/services in these cases levy fails. Circular 178/2022 has clarified on non taxability-circular binding on dept officers Dhiren Chemicals [2002 (143) ELT 19 (SC)]

10. Exports of service paid for in CFE treated as taxable to GST alleging POS is India
Agreement/SOWs would be paramount to establish nature of services. Proof of deliverables such as reports/emails submitted to foreign clients. This is more seen in alleging outsourced support services[POS as per section 13(2) location of foreign recipient client] to be intermediary services[taxable as POS vide section 13(8) of IGST Act is location of Indian supplier].

Plethora of favourable decisions are there in erstwhile ST laws and thereafter as well to support auditee. In Ohmi Industries Asia Pvt. Ltd. vs. Assistant Commissioner '[TS-128-HC(DEL)-2023-GST] HC: held assessee not 'intermediary' for provision of services to Japanese affiliate, allows IGST refund.

Conclusion

Where the stakes are high, the assessee is also suggested to consult with expert professionals in indirect taxes and GST, and based on their opinion, take a call to contest orpay voluntarily[wherever valid liability is there].

In order to avoid any surprises during audit, it is also suggested to get pre-audit done internally / externally by competent professional CA's. During pre-audit if any valid tax liability omitted/ unpaid found out [such as RCM on import of services/GTA services], discharge voluntarily with interest[to avoid penalty- if found in course of dept audit].

In this article the paper writer has given practical issues and the replies which if properly drafted could certainly help to avoid/reduce frivolous objections and relief by way of dropping of demands at the stage of audit itself[prior to SCN].

Article has been contributed by CA Roopa Nayak

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

2020: AT1 bonds written off. 2023: Bombay HC says no. 2026: Supreme Court agrees. What a journey.

The Yes Bank AT1 bond story is one of the most interesting chapters in Indian banking and investing.

Here is what happened:

→ March 2020: Yes Bank was placed under a moratorium. Withdrawals were restricted to ₹50,000, with limited exceptions allowing up to ₹5 lakh for specified emergencies.

→ The moratorium was supposed to run until April 3, but the reconstruction happened quickly and the new board took charge on March 26.

→ As part of the rescue, ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank AT1 bonds were written down to zero. AT1 bonds are not normal FDs or ordinary bonds. They are designed to absorb losses when a bank gets into serious trouble.

→ The problem was that many retail investors claimed they had been mis-sold these AT1 bonds as something similar to an FD.

SEBI's investigation records complaints where investors said relationship managers told them the bonds were safer than FDs, or even persuaded them to break an FD and invest in AT1 bonds.

→ There was another controversial chapter involving the erstwhile Reliance Mutual Fund, now Nippon India Mutual Fund.

SEBI later investigated investments made during the Reliance Capital era. The regulator alleged a possible quid pro quoinvolving Yes Bank's lending to Reliance Group companies. The amounts and allegations have evolved through different regulatory and investigative proceedings, so this should not be treated as a finally established finding against every person involved.

→ In 2023, the Bombay High Court quashed the AT1 write-off, holding that the administrator did not have the required authority under the final reconstruction scheme to wipe out the bonds.

→ Yes Bank, RBI and the Government challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.

→ And today, 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court dismissed those appeals and upheld the Bombay High Court judgment. The ₹8,415 crore write-off has therefore been held legally invalid.

So what does this mean?

A big day for AT1 bondholders.

Especially for investors who were genuinely mis-sold these instruments as “safe”.

A difficult day for Yes Bank.

The bank now faces the consequences of a judgment that restores the bondholders' claims.

And an interesting development for SMBC.

Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation acquired 20% of Yes Bank in 2025 and subsequently increased its holding, with RBI approval for up to 24.99%.

And yes, Nippon India MF investors who were affected by the AT1 write-off also stand to benefit from the court ruling, subject to how the judgment is implemented and the amounts ultimately recoverable.

The biggest lesson for investors?

“Bond” does not mean “safe”.

And a product being sold by a bank relationship manager does not make it an FD.

AT1 bonds were created precisely because they can absorb losses when a bank gets into trouble.

This case also shows something else:
Courts can sometimes change an outcome that risk managers, regulators and investors thought was already settled.

How I ($1MM/year seller) find winning Amazon FBA products in 2026

Quick context: ~9 years selling on Amazon, 3 brands, ~1,500 SKUs (mostly toys & games), 3 VAs, $1MM/year at ~40% margin. Numbers verified by https://t.co/HnGPqhlwMu and the mods of r/FulfillmentByAmazon: https://t.co/e14qmNmwm5

Below is the process my team and I use to find products. I've broken down a bunch of Amazon stores over the last few months, and the same process keeps working for me, so here it is. No tool needed to start, just Amazon and a spreadsheet.

STEP 1 - Start from stores that already win, not from keywords or individual products

• Keyword tools tell you what people search for. They don't tell you who makes money.
• Individual products also don't tell the whole story - I have 1,500 SKUs, most of them don't make much money, but combined they made me a business.
• Find brands that started recently (6-12 months) and already sell well - that proves the niche is still open to new entrants
• Amazon's own "X+ bought in past month" on each listing, summed across their ASINs, gives you a revenue estimate that's surprisingly close

STEP 2 - Ask ONE question: where did the founder add value ?

• Almost everything on Amazon is made by the same Chinese factories. If the only thing you add is a logo, you're competing on price - and that's a race to zero margin
• The products I keep seeing with HIGH margins are ones where the customer pays for something made once and sold many times: a DESIGN (puzzles, card games, kitchen gadgets with a cute/creative shape), or a product paired with an app/course
• People buy a puzzle for the picture, not the cardboard. That's why a $3 puzzle sells for $20 - same goes for card games, posters, or anything like that
• This is my framework from running my own brand, not something I can prove - but the stores I analyse fit it a lot
• I stay away from food and supplements - no experience there, so I won't pretend to advise on them (but they do essentially follow the same pattern - create a good recipe once and sell the food many times)

STEP 3 - Work out the real margin (this kills 80% of ideas)

Per-unit economics for the store you're looking at:

• Revenue = "bought in past month" x price, for every ASIN
• COGS = ask 3-5 suppliers on Alibaba for a quote on the same product at 100 MOQ. Real quotes, not guesses
• FBA fees + 15% referral fee - Amazon's revenue calculator does this
• PPC = CPC x monthly search volume x estimated CTR, for the keywords they bid on
• What's left is profit. I mostly ignore anything that ends up under ~25% margin

STEP 4 - Check how they get their sales

• Almost no PPC and still selling? The product itself converts. Great sign.
• Bringing traffic from outside of Amazon ? You'll have to understand if you can replicate their methods
• Sales spread across many SKUs, or one hero SKU ? One hero SKU = you have to win one fight. Many SKUs = they have a design pipeline you'd have to match

STEP 5 - Price the validation, not the dream

• Estimate how much it would cost you to test each brand you're thinking of launching. At the end of the day, in order to succeed, you'll need multiple tries (nobody has a 100% success rate). You want to try as many businesses as possible, as quickly as possible, for as cheap as possible.
• Cost to test = MOQ (e.g. 100 units x $5.40 = $540) + shipping + ONE month of ads on a few long tail keywords
• Some products you might be able to POD (print on demand) - that is, only *produce* the product AFTER you get the order. This is NOT dropshipping. You might even have to do it at a loss per order. This is just to validate demand. If you see there is demand for your product - shut off the listing and go produce it in China.
• If you can't test it for well under your budget, it's not a validation, it's a bet

WHY AM I GIVING THIS AWAY ?

• Fair question - I'd ask it too
• I used to think I should keep the good niches "secret". I don't anymore - people who know how to research will find them either way, and there's still a LOT of work and risk to take before any niche pays you.
• There's a huge amount of good niches to get into, but an even huger amount of niches that will DEFINITELY lose you money.
• I see Amazon newbies making the most basic mistakes all the time - because they don't understand that they gotta ADD VALUE to make money.
• What do I get out of it ? Nothing right now. Go check for yourself - the website and the case studies are completely free. You will see why the products there make money - they are good products where the founder added value to their customers' lives.
• The site is free to browse, no paywall

All the case studies are on my website, https://t.co/UvYlJ6HVeE (disclosure: I built it). It's more in depth than my posts - suppliers, keywords they rank/advertise on, graphs, etc.

Statement : SBI has told the stock exchanges about its data breach, but not the customers whose data was leaked

New Delhi, 21 October 2026

Today, the State Bank of India told the BSE and the National Stock Exchange, in a disclosure under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, that it has experienced an incident involving the loss of customer data. On 16 October 2026 the bank received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In that its customers’ data was available on the dark web. Its preliminary analysis of about 3.75 lakh records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. These include registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs and details linked to loan records. The bank says it does not yet know where the data came from, and it has engaged a CERT-In empanelled agency to find out.

SBI did not detect this breach itself and learnt of it from outside agencies after the data had already been published. On the same day, a threat monitoring account on X flagged a claim by a group calling itself “Siriusim” that it had released 3.75 lakh rows of SBI data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. The bank’s disclosure does not mention these documents. It also does not say what the remaining records, beyond the 3,897 it has identified, contain.

At the time of this statement, SBI has not said that it has informed any of the affected customers, and its disclosure is silent on the point. Five days passed between the alert and today’s filing. The filing assures investors that the incident has no material impact on the bank’s operations, financial performance or business continuity. However, it does not state anything to the 3,897 people whose phone numbers, dates of birth and home addresses are now with fraudsters. These customers are the most likely to receive calls from persons posing as SBI officials who can recite their account details back to them. A customer cannot guard against a fraud she has not been warned of.

The Internet Freedom Foundation calls on SBI to inform every affected customer directly and without further delay.

We regret to note that the law in force today does not compel the bank to do so. Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary to intimate a personal data breach to the Data Protection Board and to each affected Data Principal, and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 prescribes how this is to be done. But the Union Government chose a staggered commencement, and these provisions will take effect only on 13 May 2027, nearly four years after Parliament enacted the law. The reporting obligations that apply today, under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 and the RBI’s cyber security framework for banks, are owed to regulators and not to customers. A listed bank is bound to keep the stock exchanges informed. No law in force clearly binds it to inform the people whose data it holds.

Our demands

1. SBI must inform each affected customer by SMS, email and letter to the registered address, in English, Hindi and the language of the customer’s branch, stating what data was exposed and what steps they should take. It should open a dedicated helpline and an online facility for customers to check whether their data is affected.

2. SBI must state what the 3.75 lakh records and the 2,722 documents contain, how many customers they relate to, and whether they include KYC documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or passport copies.

3. When the investigation concludes, SBI must disclose how the data left its systems, including whether it came through a vendor or a direct selling agent, and publish a summary of the investigating agency’s findings.

4. The Reserve Bank of India should direct all regulated entities to notify customers of personal data breaches within a fixed period, pending the commencement of the DPDP Act.

5. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology should bring Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules into force immediately.

Title: Let Us Not Be in Denial, Disenfranchisement Is Real

The article by Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav examines whether the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has resulted in the exclusion of eligible voters in India. Its central argument is that voter-list discrepancies cannot be dismissed as administrative errors without rigorous verification.

Introduction

The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is an exercise conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI) to verify and update electoral rolls. The objective is to remove duplicate or ineligible entries and ensure that eligible citizens are registered. However, the authors argue that the process may also exclude genuine voters, undermining universal adult suffrage.

Main Facts in Details

* Electoral roll discrepancies: The article compares projected adult populations with voter numbers on the SIR lists across nine states.

* Estimated shortfall: The accompanying table reports a combined gap of approximately 7.06 crore between projected adult population and the listed voters across these states.

* Uttar Pradesh: The table estimates a shortfall of 2.77 crore, or 17.1% of its projected adult population.

* Bihar: The estimated gap is 88 lakh, equivalent to 10.6%.

* National implications: The authors argue that if similar discrepancies exist elsewhere, the number of eligible voters missing from electoral rolls could be substantial.

These figures represent an estimated population-to-voter gap, not a verified count of disenfranchised citizens. Differences may also arise from demographic projections, migration, mortality and eligibility factors.

Core Challenges

* Administrative exclusion: Eligible citizens may be omitted during verification.

* Transparency deficit: Inadequate public audits can weaken confidence in electoral rolls.

* Democratic legitimacy: Exclusion of eligible voters undermines political equality and representation.

* Accountability: The ECI must distinguish legitimate deletions from erroneous removals.

Constructive Criticism

The article challenges the argument that missing voter entries are insignificant simply because electoral rolls may previously have contained duplicate or outdated names. Both over-registration and under-registration require evidence-based scrutiny. However, population estimates alone cannot establish the precise number of wrongful exclusions.

Way Forward

* Conduct independent, state-wise audits of electoral rolls.

* Publish transparent data on additions, deletions and reasons for removal.

* Provide accessible correction, appeal and grievance-redressal mechanisms.

* Strengthen booth-level verification while protecting citizens from arbitrary exclusion.

Highlighted Keywords

Universal Adult Suffrage, Electoral Integrity, Disenfranchisement, Electoral Roll Revision, Procedural Justice, Democratic Legitimacy, Accountability, Evidence-Based Governance.

Conclusion

Electoral integrity requires both clean voter lists and the protection of every eligible citizen's voting rights. The fundamental democratic principle is clear: no eligible voter should lose the right to vote because of administrative failure.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

The PCI Managing Committee strongly opposes these instances of blatant executive overreach and demands that the authorities respect citizens' and journalists' fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression enshrined in and protected by Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution.

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

UPDATE: 14-year-old e-bike rider dies; West Melbourne store owner now charged with second-degree murder

The 14-year-old boy police say was intentionally struck by a West Melbourne store owner last week has died, and the man accused of hitting him is now charged with second-degree murder.

With the family's consent, the West Melbourne Police Department has identified the teen as Hunter Russey of West Melbourne.

According to police, the case began around 4:30 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, when 32-year-old Kavan Vishnubhai Patel, who owns the Corner Store at 100 South Wickham Road, received an alarm alert and saw on surveillance video that the store's front glass door had been broken. Patel told officers he saw someone leave the area on an e-bike.

Police say Patel followed the rider in his vehicle and intentionally struck him along Cocoanut Grove Avenue after the encounter at the store had ended. Investigators say Patel left Hunter on the side of the road without rendering aid, returned to the store, and did not tell responding officers he had hit him. Hunter was later found unresponsive in a roadside ditch.

Hunter was taken to Holmes Regional Medical Center as a trauma alert with severe injuries and was later transferred to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children, where he remained on life support.

According to police, Hunter's family made the decision to remove him from life support on the evening of Saturday, October 17. He died at 11:46 p.m. His family has chosen to donate his organs to help others.

Patel was originally charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Following Hunter's death, investigators obtained an arrest warrant, and Patel was rearrested just after 10 a.m. Sunday. He is now charged with second-degree murder and is being held at the Brevard County Jail without bond.

The West Melbourne Police Department offered condolences to Hunter's family and friends and said it will continue working the case and provide prosecutors with the evidence needed to move forward.

The family has asked that the public respect their privacy.
